platforms.title: Chilblains: 3 Warming Mistakes That Make Itchy Toes Worse
platforms.meta_description: Red, itchy, swollen toes after the cold are usually chilblains, not frostbite. Why they happen, 3 warming mistakes to drop, and when to see a GP.
platforms.body_html:
You get home after a wet walk, kick off your boots and prop your cold feet against the radiator. A few hours later your toes are puffy, pinkish-purple and so itchy you can't stop rubbing them. It feels like a mild case of frostbite, but it is a different thing. Chilblains are small, itchy, inflamed patches that appear after cold exposure without the skin ever freezing. The NHS describes them as patches that usually show up a few hours after you have been in the cold, mostly on the fingers and toes, though the face and legs can be affected too. The skin can itch or feel like it is burning, and it may turn red or purple, which can be harder to see on brown and black skin.

What is going on under the skin

The NHS explains the mechanism in two steps. Cold makes the small blood vessels in your fingers and toes narrow, so blood moves less easily. Then, as you warm up, the deeper vessels stay narrow while the vessels nearer the surface widen, and that mismatch causes the pain, itching and colour change. That is why sudden heat on cold skin is part of the problem rather than the cure.

A large case series from the Mayo Clinic gives a picture of who gets them. Cappel and Wetter reviewed the records of 104 patients with chilblains (pernio) seen between 2000 and 2011 and published the results in 2014. Their average age at diagnosis was 38.3, 79% were women, and the toes were affected in 82% of patients, against 30% for the fingers. A smaller study from the same clinic (Shahi and colleagues, 2015) looked at 5 patients who had vascular testing, and all 5 showed vessel spasm when their hands were put in ice water. That supports the idea that an over-reactive response to cold is part of the story.

Drop these 3 warming mistakes

Mistake 1: putting your feet on the radiator or under hot water. The NHS is direct about this: do not warm cold hands or feet on a radiator or under hot water. Instead, dry the skin and warm it slowly if you have been exposed to the cold.

Mistake 2: staying in damp socks and shoes. The NHS advises avoiding cold or damp conditions where you can, and if you do go out, wearing warm, waterproof clothing, gloves and thick socks. Damp is part of the trigger, not just low temperatures, so changing out of wet socks and shoes as soon as you get in matters.

Mistake 3: smoking, caffeine and decongestants. According to the NHS, smoking, drinks that contain caffeine and medicine for a blocked nose (decongestants) can affect the flow of blood in your fingers and toes, so it is worth avoiding them while you have chilblains. The NHS also says not to scratch or pick at the skin. A pharmacist can suggest a lotion to soothe the itching.

The Mayo Clinic series is a useful reality check here. Of the 28 patients with follow-up data, 23 (82%) had a complete response to conservative care such as warming, drying and stopping smoking. It was a retrospective review with no comparison group, so it cannot prove those steps work on their own, but it shows how far simple measures went in practice.

What about tablets? The NHS says a GP may sometimes prescribe a medicine that widens the blood vessels. The usual choice has been nifedipine, a blood pressure drug. A 1989 study (Rustin and colleagues) reported that it shortened the time lesions took to clear. But a 2016 randomised, double-blind crossover trial in primary care (Souwer and colleagues) gave 32 people with chronic chilblains nifedipine 60 mg a day for 6 weeks and found no significant difference from placebo, while blood pressure dropped and swelling was more common on the drug. Medication is a decision for your GP, not a first step.

Most chilblains settle on their own

The NHS says chilblains usually go away by themselves in 2 to 3 weeks. Some cases need a closer look, though. In the Mayo Clinic group, 4% of patients had an associated connective tissue disease and 3% an associated blood cancer. The NHS advises seeing a GP if your skin is not getting better after 2 to 3 weeks, if there is pus coming out of your skin, if your temperature is very high or you feel hot, cold or shivery, if you keep getting chilblains, or if you have diabetes, because foot problems can be more serious. A GP may refer you for tests if it is not clear why they keep happening. This article is general health information and does not replace advice from a clinician who has examined you.

So tonight, peel off the damp socks first, dry your feet and let them warm up slowly at room temperature before you go anywhere near the radiator.

Sources: NHS, "Chilblains" (reviewed April 2026); Cappel JA, Wetter DA, Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 2014; Shahi V et al., Dermatology, 2015; Rustin MH et al., British Journal of Dermatology, 1989; Souwer IH et al., Annals of Family Medicine, 2016.
